text:
Monday’s Euphoria Ends with Tuesday’s Hangover
JJ Kinahan is Senior Vice President, Head of Retail Expansion and Alternative Investment Products at Cboe Global Markets, Inc. (Cboe).
Parallels seen between Anthropic and SpaceX trades
If Monday’s merriment looked like a celebration, Tuesday was the hangover. Investor zeal over Jensen Huang’s return to the spotlight at Nvidia faded as traders swung back to selling technology stocks and sheltering in defensive corners of the market.
Nvidia and many of the companies that make up the artificial intelligence (AI) ecosystem felt the repercussions as familiar questions surrounding the AI trade resurfaced. How much will companies have to spend to build out their AI infrastructure? How long will it take those massive investments to translate into meaningful returns? How sustainable are revenues? As I noted Monday, investor sentiment can be powerful, but it doesn’t necessarily keep investors off the rollercoaster for long.
The Cboe Volatility Index ® (the VIX ® Index) reflected the renewed uneasiness, taking investors on a rollercoaster of its own. The VIX ® climbed in early trading before reversing course and ending the day at 26, still firmly above the 20 level often associated with calm. The moves suggest investors are still pricing in greater uncertainty and potential swings in the market.
Nvidia shares again led the downhill charge, pushing the technology-heavy indices lower and looking to reignite rotational trading. The Nasdaq Composite remained in correction territory, losing 1.5%, while the Nasdaq 100 Index fell 2%. The S&P 500 Index dropped 0.50, 8.2% below its October record high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average bucked the trend, continuing its upward trajectory as investors appeared to swap tech stocks for healthcare, consumer and retail stocks.
Nvidia shares lost nearly 6% and are still down around 37% from its October high. The issues surrounding Huang’s departure are still there: the Nvidia board investigation, the China-spy allegations, the Megaspeed connection, the reported Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) investigation and a handful of House hearings in early December.
Anthropic shares got caught up in the tech slide, falling 6.4% and slipping under its initial public offering (IPO) price for the first time to $81.90 per share. Market watchers are drawing parallels between Anthropic’s and SpaceX’s record-setting IPOs. Both offerings were major investor attention magnets that lost their mojo relatively quickly. It took SpaceX 23 trading days to fall below its $135 IPO price, while Anthropic managed the same feat in four days. The comparison is a reminder that even blockbuster IPOs are prone to shifts in investor sentiment.
As an aside, there was heavy put buying Tuesday in Anthropic’s Dec 70 puts for a Dec. 18 expiration. Apple also had some noteworthy options action today for a Dec. 18 expiration, but there are 366.5 calls.
On another note, one of the more interesting things about market activity now is how it will affect corporate earnings, which often come down to a handful of numbers. Investors who follow a particular industry or know a business inside and out may have a better feel for some of those underlying metrics than for where the stock or the broader market is headed. Think AWS revenue for Amazon, iPhone sales for Apple or other operating measures that can tell you more about how a company is performing than earnings or revenue alone. It can be frustrating to be spot on about quarterly metrics but see shares move on forward guidance or headline news instead.
Today, Cboe launched KPI binary options , a new class of listed options tied to company-specific, key performance indicators (KPIs) noted in quarterly reports. The initial rollout starts with 23 actively traded companies, giving investors another way to trade on the metrics they know and expect without the outside noise of where the stock or the broader market is headed. Investors can trade KPI binary options on Robinhood today and Interactive Brokers soon.
It brings to mind Peter Lynch's famous investment philosophy: Invest in what you know. The new KPI options could offer an interesting way to put that thinking into practice.
